title: NASA's New Telescope Could See What Even James Webb Can't
summary:
The James Webb Space Telescope is famous for seeing deep into space. But there's a whole type of light it can't see — and NASA wants to build a telescope that can.

It's called PRIMA, short for Probe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics. NASA just announced it's moving forward with the design. If everything goes well, it could launch in 2033 and run for five years.

Here's the key difference: JWST sees near- and mid-infrared light. PRIMA will see far-infrared — longer wavelengths. Think of it like this: JWST has really good eyes, but PRIMA gets a whole new pair of glasses that lets it see colors JWST misses.

What will it look at? Planets being born, galaxies growing, and giant black holes changing over time. "We can't actually address these science questions with JWST," said Meredith MacGregor, a scientist at Johns Hopkins University, "because the spectral lines that are required are only in the far-infrared."

PRIMA's telescope mirror is 5.9 feet (1.8 meters) wide. The mission costs about $1.2 billion — way less than JWST's $10 billion. It's the first of a new class called Probe Explorers, sitting between giant flagship missions and smaller ones.

One scientist said he's most excited about "the things I don't yet know." Same here!
why_it_matters: New telescopes keep adding to what humans can see, so the space questions kids ask today may be the ones scientists answer with the next big mission.

background_read: NASA (the United States space agency) launched the James Webb Space Telescope in 2021. It orbits far from Earth and studies infrared light, which our eyes cannot see.

Infrared is invisible light with longer waves than red light, and far-infrared has even longer waves. Most far-infrared light is blocked by Earth's atmosphere, so a telescope looking for it has to be in space.
Johns Hopkins University (a research university in Maryland, USA) is where scientist Meredith MacGregor works. She says JWST simply cannot pick up the spectral lines that only appear in far-infrared.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA, working with scientists such as Meredith MacGregor at Johns Hopkins University.
WHAT: NASA announced it is moving forward with the design of PRIMA, a new far-infrared space telescope.
WHERE: In space — it could launch in 2033, with a mirror 1.8 meters (5.9 feet) wide.
WHY: Because JWST cannot see the far-infrared spectral lines needed to study planets being born, galaxies growing, and black holes changing.
